newsitem.title: USA: POLL - US yld curve seen flatter in 97, steeper '98.
newsitem.headline: POLL - US yld curve seen flatter in 97, steeper '98.

text.p: The U.S. yield curve is expected to flatten through the rest of the year and then shift back to a steepening gear by mid-1998, the latest Reuters quartely U.S. economic survey showed.

Yield curve forecasts for 1997 follow expectations the economy will likely pick up some steam in the second half of the year, which could in turn prompt the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy before the end of 1997.

"What the consensus (survey) is trying to tell you is that the economy is going to be performing well over the next several quarters," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
"We'll probably see mild upward movement in the rate of inflation and we'll probably see some additional Fed tightening in monetary policy, but nothing dramatic," the Daiwa chief economist added.
The economy would then cool off -- partly due to the expected Fed credit squeeze -- easing inflation fears and bringing interest rates back down.
"The yield curve will probably flatten with the expected additional Fed tightening.
"But then in the latter part of next year ... you'll start to see the economy settle down, short rates will fall more than long rates and the curve will steepen again," Moran said.
The Reuters survey showed Wall Street pundits saw the rates on U.S. three-month bills averaging 5.29 percent in the third quarter of 1997.

That rate is then expected to creep up gradually to an expected 5.61 percent peak in the second quarter of 1998, when it is expected to begin to fall again to around 5.30 percent in the second quarter of 1999.

Meanwhile, the yield on the two-year note is seen at 6.19 percent in the third quarter of 1997, peaking at 6.42 percent in the first quarter of 1998 and sliding back to 6.03 percent by the second quarter of 1999.
For the long end of the curve, Wall Street forecasters see the U.S. 30-year bond yield at 6.80 percent in the third quarter of 1997.

That rate was then seen peaking in the fourth quarter of 1997 at 6.90 percent, remaining at those lofty levels in the first quarter of 1998 and then slipping back to 6.75 percent by the second quarter of 1999.

"The timing that is reflected in this consensus is about right, but maybe the long end will have to back up in yield a bit more than the survey consensus indicates," said Patrick Dimick, bond strategist at UBS Securities LLC.

Analysts said the performance of the U.S. yield curve has gained special attention recently, mainly after the Fed decided to leave interest rates unchanged at the last Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on July 1 and 2.
Wall Streeters said the Fed appeared to be relying more on market rates to regulate the speed at which the economy is, or will be, running.

"In terms of economic growth, the Fed likes to let market rates do most of the work. It's sort of a self-correcting processs," said David Jones, vice chairman and chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co Inc.
Jones also said it appeared that the Fed now feels it has plenty of time to act given the nature of the current economic expansion.
"(The Fed) would tend to follow the markets rather than lead them in this current circumstance of solid growth, low unemployment, and low inflation," Jones said.
